exchanges.text: Grace Liu keeps cutting people off in our product syncs. how do I handle it without making it awkward

In the moment, try "Hold that thought, Grace, I want to let Felix finish." It's firm but friendly. If it keeps happening, tell her privately that you'd like everyone to get a full turn, and ask her to help you model that.
Felix Wong invited me to an hour-long meeting with zero agenda. decline?
Reasonable to ask first: "Happy to join if I know what decision we're making. Could you share the goal or agenda?" If it's still vague, you can decline and ask for a short summary afterwards.
need to tell Imogen Price she missed the deadline again. dreading it

Keep it specific and curious: "The research summary was due Tuesday and it's landed late twice now. What's getting in the way?" Describing the pattern without judging her gives her room to tell you what's really going on.
and if she gets defensive?
Acknowledge her view without backing down: "I hear that, and I still need us to find a way to hit the dates." Then move on to what would help next time.
Lucia Romano wants to add a big thing to the release two days before freeze. how do I say no without burning the relationship

Try: "I want this to land well, and squeezing it in now puts the whole release at risk. Can we aim it for the next cycle and agree what's in scope today?" Offering a clear alternative makes it a redirect rather than a flat no.
Hugo Laurent never says a word in retros. he's sharp tho

Try giving people a few minutes to write thoughts down silently before discussing, since quieter people often do better that way. You could also tell Hugo beforehand which topic you'd like his view on, so he can prepare.
can you draft a quick text to Nina Kowalski, I need to push our 1:1 to tomorrow, something not curt
Here's one: "Hi Nina, something urgent has come up today and I'd like to give our 1:1 proper attention. Could we move it to tomorrow? Sorry for the shuffle, and let me know what suits you."
Arjun Mehta presented my analysis in the leadership meeting like it was his. I'm fuming

Talk to him soon, and assume it might be careless rather than deliberate: "I noticed the analysis was presented without my name on it. Next time, can we make sure it's credited?" In future, share your work in writing with the right people so the authorship is clear.
Zoe Turner and Malik Hassan disagree on the roadmap and I'm chairing tomorrow. how do I open

Start with what they share: "We all want X for customers. We differ on how to get there, so let's lay out each option and the evidence for it." Give each of them equal uninterrupted time, and end on the decision you need rather than who's right.
hybrid meeting this afternoon, Freya Lund is the only one remote. last time she was ignored
Have everyone use the same setup if you can, or at least put the screen with Freya where the room can see it. Ask her for her view first, and pause for her before moving to each new topic.
Oscar Bell keeps pushing a feature we're not doing this quarter. he asked again today

Give him the reasoning rather than just the no: "Here's what we're prioritising and why, and here's what would need to change for his idea to move up." People take a no better when they can see the logic behind it.
Rosa Jimenez hasn't replied about the user interview findings in a week. nudge text pls, friendly
Try: "Hi Rosa, just circling back on the interview findings. Even a quick reaction would help, since I'm trying to finalise the next steps. Thanks!" It's light, and it tells her why it matters.
presenting to the exec team in an hour and my hands are shaking a bit
Slow your breathing for a minute, with a longer exhale than inhale. Then settle on your one main point and say it in the first thirty seconds. If you know that, the rest will follow.
ok. what if Ethan Clarke asks something I can't answer
Say "I don't have that to hand, but I'll find out and come back to you by Friday." It sounds credible, and far better than guessing.
Yuki Tanaka's meeting is overrunning and I have to leave in 5. how to bow out
Wait for a natural pause and say, "I have to drop off at the hour, so let me share my view on this point now." Then say it and leave without apologising too much.
Callum Reid starts Monday. what should our first 1:1 cover

Keep it relaxed. Ask how he likes to work and communicate, explain what success looks like in his first 30 days, and introduce him to two or three key people. Finish by asking what would make his first week easier.
Dmitri Volkov's replies on Slack read really sharp. is it me or him

Often it's just brevity coming across as bluntness in text. Try a quick call to see how he sounds in person, and if the tone still bothers you, say so kindly: "Your short replies sometimes feel abrupt to me. Is everything okay?"
need to nudge Grace about the user interview synthesis, don't want to sound pushy

Try: "Hi Grace, how's the interview synthesis coming along? Even a rough version of the top themes would help me shape next week's priorities, so share whatever stage it's at." It asks for something small, which keeps the nudge light.
Felix invited me to a 1hr sync I really don't need to be in. polite no?

Try: "Thanks for the invite, Felix. I think I'd add more value reading the outcomes than sitting in the full hour, so could you drop the key decisions in the channel afterwards? Happy to weigh in there if anything needs my input."
Imogen ran the demo for me yesterday when I was stuck in another thing. thank you msg, make it warm but short
Try: "Imogen, thank you so much for stepping in on the demo yesterday. I heard it went really well, and it meant a lot not having to worry about it. I owe you one!"
running 10 late to the roadmap chat with Kwame
Try: "Hi Kwame, running about 10 minutes behind. Sorry! Please start without me if you like, and I'll join as soon as I can."
Lucia keeps adding stuff to the sprint. need to say no without starting a fight

Try: "Lucia, I'd love to fit this in, but the sprint is already full and adding it means something else slips. Shall we look at what we'd swap out, or put this at the top of the next sprint?" Offering a trade-off turns it into a joint decision instead of a flat no.
good, the trade-off bit is what I needed
Glad it helps. If she pushes back, repeat the trade-off calmly rather than arguing the merits of the request itself.
asking Nina for feedback on my PRD draft by thursday. keep it brief

Try: "Hi Nina, I've finished a first draft of the PRD and would really value your eyes on it. Could you share any feedback by Thursday? The open questions in section 3 are the ones I'm least sure about."
Zoe, need the funnel numbers for last month before friday for my review
Try: "Hi Zoe, could you send me last month's funnel numbers by Friday morning? I need them for a review that afternoon. A quick summary is plenty if the full breakdown is a lot of work."
have to tell Malik the release is slipping a week. he'll be annoyed

Try: "Malik, a heads-up: the release is moving back by a week because we found an issue in final testing and want to fix it properly. I know that's frustrating, and I'm happy to talk through what it means for your team's plans." Lead with the news and the reason, and don't pad it with apologies.
I'm offline friday afternoon, tell Freya in a normal non-dramatic way
Try: "Hi Freya, just so you know, I'll be offline from about 1pm on Friday. If anything needs me, shout before then and we can sort it out in the morning."
this sounds too harsh to Oscar? "Your spec is missing half the edge cases. Redo it."
It does read as blunt. Try: "Oscar, thanks for pulling the spec together. I think we need to cover more edge cases before it's ready. Could we go through a few together tomorrow?"
Rosa starts monday, welcome her in the team channel

Try: "Everyone, please give a warm welcome to Rosa Jimenez, who joins us on Monday! Rosa, we're really glad you're here. Ask us anything, however small, and we'll make your first week as easy as we can."
Ethan's bug report just says "checkout broken". need more detail from him without being rude

Try: "Thanks for flagging this, Ethan. To help us track it down, could you tell me what you were doing when it broke, which device or browser you were on, and whether you saw an error? A screenshot would be great too."
ask Yuki if we can do 10 instead of 11 tomorrow
Try: "Hi Yuki, would it be possible to start our catch-up at 10 instead of 11 tomorrow? If that doesn't work, no problem, 11 is fine as it is."
28 and sticky in the office today, no aircon. linen shirt or cotton?
Linen, as it breathes better and dries faster when you sweat. Pick a loose cut in white, pale blue or another light colour, since those hide damp patches best.
cycling in at 7:30 when it's about 11 degrees, but it'll hit 24 by 4pm. how do I dress for that
Layer up. Wear a breathable short-sleeve top with a light packable windproof jacket or a thin long-sleeve over it. Take the jacket off once it warms up and stuff it in your bag for the ride home.
showers all day, I've got a client meeting at 2. leather loafers ok?

Loafers are risky if you'll be walking through puddles, since wet leather can stain and warp. Wear waterproof boots or smart waterproof shoes for the journey and carry the loafers in a bag to change into before the meeting.
meeting with Grace Liu's team at 11, it's going to be 30. blazer or no blazer

Skip the blazer unless you know they'll all be wearing one. A crisp shirt or smart sleeveless top with tailored trousers looks professional enough, and you could carry a thin layer in case the meeting room is over-air-conditioned.
only 15 and really windy today?? it's JUNE. what do I put on
Typical British June! A light jacket that blocks the wind, like a trench or a bomber, over a long-sleeve top will do it. Trousers will be more comfortable than a skirt or dress in that wind.
rooftop drinks with the team after work, it was warm all day. will I freeze up there
Probably a bit once the sun drops, since rooftops catch the breeze. Bring a light cardigan, a denim jacket or a big scarf that you can drape over your shoulders.
scarf it is
Good choice. A cotton or linen blend one is light enough to stuff in your bag if it stays warm.
bright sun but only 17, still need sunscreen? asking cos it feels cold
Yes. UV depends on the sun, not the temperature, and in June in London it can be high even when it feels cool. Put SPF 30 or higher on your face, neck and any exposed arms.
thunderstorm warning this afternoon, I have to walk 20 mins to see Kwame Mensah. umbrella or raincoat

A raincoat with a hood is better in a thunderstorm, because gusty wind can wreck an umbrella and a tall umbrella isn't ideal in lightning. Wear quick-drying trousers and shoes you don't mind getting wet.
lunchtime run, it's 27. what do I wear so I don't die
Wear a light, loose, moisture-wicking top and shorts in light colours, along with a cap and sunglasses. Skip cotton, since it gets heavy with sweat, and slow your pace a little in that heat.
so muggy tonight I can't sleep. what should I wear to bed
Go for loose pyjamas or a big T-shirt in cotton, linen or bamboo, which wick moisture better than synthetics. Use just a sheet instead of a duvet and keep the cotton thin.
presenting to Kwame's whole department today and it's hot. I sweat when I'm nervous lol

Wear a breathable fabric like cotton or linen in a mid-tone or pattern, since both white and grey show sweat more. A lightweight undershirt can help, and a layer you can remove makes it easy to cool down before you start.
are sandals ok at work in a hot week? Hugo Laurent always looks so put together

In most offices, neat leather or minimal sandals are fine in hot weather, especially with tailored trousers or a midi dress. Keep your feet well groomed and skip anything worn out or very beachy, such as flip-flops.
grey and drizzly Friday, casual day. jeans or something lighter?
Lighter trousers in cotton or a linen blend are usually more comfortable, as jeans stay heavy and damp in drizzle. Add a light waterproof jacket and shoes with some grip for wet pavements.
it's 22 and sunny but Imogen Price says I'll still want a jacket for the walk by the river. true?

She might be right, since it's often a few degrees cooler and breezier by the water, especially in the evening. A thin jacket or cardigan that fits in your bag will cover you without being a nuisance.
got a tin of chickpeas, a lemon and some sad spinach. ideas?
Fry a crushed garlic clove in olive oil, add the drained chickpeas with cumin or smoked paprika, then wilt in the spinach and finish with lemon juice. It's good on toast or stirred through rice.
jammy eggs, how long again
Lower them into already boiling water for 6½ to 7 minutes, then straight into iced water. That gives a set white and a soft, jammy yolk that peels easily.
flat is boiling and I refuse to turn the hob on. no-cook lunch ideas?

Try a white bean salad with tinned tuna, cherry tomatoes, red onion, parsley and lots of lemon and olive oil. Or tear up burrata or mozzarella over sliced tomatoes and peaches with basil and good bread.
is it actually bad to reheat rice. I always have leftovers

It's fine if you handle it right. Cool it quickly, ideally within an hour, get it into the fridge, and eat it within a day. When you reheat it, make sure it's steaming hot all the way through, and only reheat it once.
recipe wants buttermilk for fried chicken and I have none
Stir a spoonful of lemon juice or white vinegar into milk and leave it for 5 to 10 minutes until it thickens slightly. Plain yoghurt loosened with a little milk also works well as a marinade.
Hugo brought an amazing herby couscous salad to the team lunch. draft me a text asking for the recipe, casual
Here's one you could send: "Hi Hugo, that couscous salad you brought was brilliant. Any chance you could share how you made it? I especially want to know what herbs and dressing you used."
want to prep lunches on Sunday for the week. what actually keeps ok till Friday

Cooked grains, roasted vegetables, boiled eggs and dressings keep well for three to four days. Anything that needs to last until Friday is better cooked fresh midweek or frozen, and soft herbs and leafy greens should be added on the day.
doing halloumi on the balcony bbq tonight. marinade?

Mix olive oil, lemon juice, dried oregano, garlic and a little chilli, and thread the halloumi onto skewers with courgette. Grill it until it has good char marks, then drizzle with honey while it's hot.
back from a long meeting, 10 mins to eat. I have noodles, eggs, frozen edamame

Cook the noodles with the edamame in the same pot for the last couple of minutes, and fry an egg on the side. Toss everything with soy sauce, a little sesame oil or chilli oil if you have it, and spring onion if there's any.
did my first interval session yesterday and my calves are wrecked. run today or rest?

Dull, general soreness is fine for a 20–30 minute easy jog on soft ground, which often loosens things up. If it's sharp, one-sided or makes you change your stride, rest. Either way, do slow calf raises and some gentle walking.
10k on Sunday. I always go out way too fast and die at 7k. help

Aim for the first 2 km to feel almost too easy, about 10 seconds per km slower than goal pace. Then settle into goal pace until 7k and only push in the last 3. The 'die at 7k' feeling usually comes from borrowing too much in the first kilometre.
hips are so tight from sitting in back to back meetings. one yoga thing I can do on my floor in 5 mins?

Try a low lunge with your back knee down. Sink your hips forward and hold for 60–90 seconds a side, breathing slowly. Follow it with a figure-four stretch on your back for another minute or so each side.
can you write a text to Grace, I'll be 10 mins late to run club thurs, tell them to go ahead without me
Here's a draft: "Hi Grace, I'll be about 10 mins late to run club on Thursday, so please start without me. I'll catch up on the route!"
my bike chain is squeaking like mad after the rain this week

It's probably dry and needs cleaning and re-lubing. Wipe off the grime with a rag and some degreaser, let it dry, then put one small drop of wet lube on each link while turning the pedals backwards. Wipe off the excess afterwards, as too much lube attracts dirt.
keep getting a stitch about 15 mins into runs

It often helps to breathe out deeply as the foot opposite the sore side lands, and to slow down briefly. Try not to eat or drink much in the hour before running, and sip rather than gulp mid-run. Working on core strength can also make stitches less frequent over time.
saddle sore after a 60k ride at the weekend, ouch. fixes?

Wear clean padded cycling shorts with nothing underneath, and apply chamois cream before long rides. Check that your saddle isn't tilted up or down, and stand on the pedals briefly every 15–20 minutes to give yourself a break. If it's still painful when you're off the bike, let it heal for a few days before riding again.
hay fever is killing my runs rn

Pollen peaks in the early morning and early evening, so midday or just after rain can be better. Wear wraparound sunglasses, rinse your face and hair when you get home, and change your clothes straight away. A pharmacist can recommend a non-drowsy antihistamine if it's getting really bad.
can't switch off at night. any yoga to wind down before bed?

Try ten minutes of slow, floor-based poses: child's pose, a gentle seated forward fold, a reclined twist, then legs up the wall for 3–5 minutes. Keep the lights low and make your exhales longer than your inhales, as that helps calm the nervous system.
first 18k long run on Saturday. do I need gels or is that overkill

For about 90 minutes of running or more, it's worth taking something. One gel or a handful of chews around 40–45 minutes, and another at about 80, is a good rule of thumb. Try them on this run rather than on race day, so you know your stomach is fine with them.
joining Felix's group ride on sunday, I've never ridden in a group. tips?

Keep a steady line and avoid sudden braking, using light touches on the brakes instead. Call out or point to hazards like potholes, and keep your hands near the brakes when you're close to someone's wheel. Leave a bike length at first and tighten up as you get more comfortable.
should I ride at the front?

Best to sit mid-pack on your first ride, where you can watch what others do and still shelter from the wind. Tell Felix beforehand that you're new, and nobody will expect you to take a turn at the front.
everyone says run slower on easy days but it feels so slow. how slow is slow

A good test is whether you can speak in full sentences without gasping. For most people that's 60–90 seconds per km slower than 10k race pace. It may feel too slow, but it lets you recover enough to hit the harder sessions properly.
just finished Piranesi and I'm bereft. what next

For a similar dreamlike, puzzle-box feel, try The Starless Sea by Erin Morgenstern. If you'd like something quieter and more human, Station Eleven by Emily St. John Mandel has the same sense of wonder.
finished Slow Horses. what's the next thing to watch
The Night Manager is a polished British spy drama with a similar sense of moral murkiness. For more dry office humour, Line of Duty is gripping and has the same grubby bureaucratic edge.
doing a 10k on sunday. podcast or music?

For an easy, steady pace, a podcast helps the miles pass, especially a story-driven one like Serial or a chatty show. If you're planning to push the pace, music with a strong beat usually works better.
is Shogun worth it? heard it's slow
It is a slow burn, but the politics, the visuals and the performances reward your patience. It's built around tension in conversations rather than constant action.
how many episodes
The first season is 10 episodes, and it tells a fairly complete story, so you don't need to commit to more.
Inspired by Cagan or Continuous Discovery Habits first?
Start with Inspired for the big picture of how strong product teams work. Then read Continuous Discovery Habits by Teresa Torres, which is more hands-on about running regular customer conversations.
something calm to fall asleep to. not true crime pls
Try Sleep With Me, where the host tells meandering, deliberately dull stories in a soothing voice. Nothing much happens is another good one, with gentle, slow narration about small everyday moments.
Felix Wong keeps telling me to watch Perfect Days. what even is it

It's a 2023 film by Wim Wenders about a man in Tokyo who cleans public toilets and finds quiet joy in his routines, music and small moments. It's slow and gentle rather than plot-driven, so it suits a calm evening.
short literary book i can finish in a weekend?
Small Things Like These by Claire Keegan is only about 110 pages and quietly powerful. Her novella Foster is similar in length and just as good.
Kwame says I have to start Succession. worth it if I don't like unlikeable characters

Nearly everyone in it is awful, but the writing is so sharp and funny that it works as a dark comedy. Give it three or four episodes, because that's when most people either get hooked or know it isn't for them.
Project Hail Mary or The Three-Body Problem for the weekend?

Project Hail Mary by Andy Weir is the easier, faster read, with plenty of humour and heart. The Three-Body Problem is more cerebral and slower to build, so choose it if you want something that makes you think.
ser vs estar, I keep mixing them up. quick rule?

Use ser for what something is: identity, origin, profession, lasting traits ("Soy de Londres", "Es alta"). Use estar for how or where something is right now: mood, condition, location ("Estoy cansada", "Está en la oficina").
Rosa helped me with the user research notes today. want to thank her in Spanish, something warm but not over the top
Try: "¡Mil gracias por tu ayuda hoy, Rosa! Me facilitaste mucho el trabajo." It's friendly and natural, and "mil gracias" is a common way to say thanks a lot.
told Hugo I was "embarazada" because I felt awkward about something. he laughed a lot. what did I actually say

"Embarazada" means pregnant, so that's the surprise. To say you felt embarrassed, use "Me dio vergüenza" or "Estaba avergonzada". It's one of the best-known false friends in Spanish, so you're in good company.
subjunctive is melting my brain. when do I actually need it

Mostly after expressions of wish, doubt, emotion or request, joined by "que" when the subject changes: "Quiero que vengas", "Espero que te guste", "No creo que sea fácil". If you're stating plain fact, you usually don't need it. Start by memorising a few triggers like "espero que" and "quiero que".
it's boiling in London today. how do I say that in Spanish
For the weather, say "Hace mucho calor hoy en Londres." To say you personally feel hot, use "Tengo calor". Don't say "Estoy caliente", which means something quite different.
ha, noted. thanks
Easy mistake to make, and a useful one to have caught early.
tú or usted with Rosa's manager? haven't met yet

For a first contact with someone senior you haven't met, "usted" is the safe choice in most Spanish-speaking settings. They'll often invite you to switch with "puedes tutearme". Spain's workplaces tend to be more relaxed than Latin America's, so if the tone is casual you could follow their lead.
what's "roadmap" and "stakeholders" in Spanish, for a call with Lucia's team

"Roadmap" is often "hoja de ruta", though many tech teams just say "roadmap". "Stakeholders" is commonly "partes interesadas" or "interesados", though again the English word is widely used in product circles. It's worth asking which they prefer.
how do j, ll and ñ sound? I keep getting them wrong

"J" is a breathy sound from the back of the throat, like a strong English "h" ("trabajo"). "Ñ" sounds like the "ny" in "canyon" ("año"). "Ll" is usually like an English "y" ("calle"), though some regions make it closer to "j" in "jam".
greeting a Spanish colleague in chat, is "hola" too plain? want something a bit more natural
"Hola" is perfectly fine, but you can add warmth with "¡Hola! ¿Qué tal?" or "¿Cómo andas?". "Buenas" is a casual, widely used shortcut at any time of day, and "¡Buenos días!" suits a morning message.
preterite vs imperfect, when to use which

Use the preterite for completed actions with a clear endpoint ("Ayer llamé a Felix"). Use the imperfect for background, habits and ongoing situations ("Llamaba a Felix cada lunes", "Hacía sol"). In a story, the imperfect sets the scene and the preterite moves the plot along.
what does "tener ganas de" mean? Rosa said it twice

It means to feel like doing something or be looking forward to it: "Tengo ganas de salir a correr" means "I feel like going for a run". Spanish uses "tener" for many states English does with "to be", like "tener sueño" (sleepy), "tener hambre" (hungry) and "tener razón" (right).
Kwame used "ojalá" in a message and I had to guess. meaning?

"Ojalá" means something like "I hope" or "if only", and it comes from Arabic. It's followed by the subjunctive: "Ojalá llueva mañana" means "I hope it rains tomorrow". With the imperfect subjunctive it becomes wistful: "Ojalá pudiera ir" means "If only I could go".
what's the Spanish for "lol" in texts? Imogen's friend writes "jaja" constantly

"Jaja" is exactly it, since the Spanish "j" sounds like an English "h". You'll also see "jajaja" for more laughter and "jeje" for a mischievous giggle. In texts, "q" often stands for "que" and "xq" for "porque".
monstera has two yellow lower leaves, panic or normal?

One or two older lower leaves yellowing now and then is usually normal ageing, so no need to panic. If several go yellow at once, check whether the soil stays soggy for days, because overwatering is the usual cause.
slugs have destroyed my hostas again. what actually works

Nematode slug control watered onto damp soil is the most effective, and it's safe for wildlife. Beyond that, going out after dark with a torch and removing them by hand, plus keeping pots raised and the area tidy, helps. Copper tape works better on pots than on beds.
orchid finished flowering, just a bare stalk now. bin it?

Definitely not, it's just resting. If the stalk is still green, cut it just above a node (the little bump) to maybe get a side spike. If it's brown and dry, trim it near the base. Keep watering lightly and it should flower again in several months.
Imogen's pothos is gigantic and I want a cutting. can you word a text, keep it breezy
Try: "Hi Imogen! Your pothos is magnificent. Would you mind if I took a cutting next time I'm over? I promise to look after it. Happy to bring a jar of water!"
is it too late to prune my lavender? it's June
Not at all. Wait until the flowers fade, then trim off the spent flower stems and a little of the green growth beneath. Avoid cutting into the old bare wood, as it rarely regrows.
fiddle leaf fig has brown crispy patches on a few leaves. it's in the brightest room

Brown crispy patches in a very bright room often mean scorch from direct midday sun, or irregular watering. Move it a little back from the glass so it gets bright but filtered light. Water thoroughly when the top few centimetres of soil are dry, rather than little and often.
heatwave this week. how often should I water the pots on the patio

In hot spells, containers may need a good soak every day, especially small terracotta pots and hanging baskets. Water early morning or in the evening so less is lost to evaporation, and aim at the soil, not the leaves. If the top is bone dry, check a finger-depth down before deciding.
greenfly all over the new rose buds ugh

Rub or squash them off with your fingers, or blast them with a jet of water. For a bigger outbreak, a spray of diluted soapy water works. Ladybirds and hoverflies will soon move in if you avoid harsh insecticides.
my echeveria has gone all tall and stretched with gaps between the leaves

That's etiolation, meaning it's reaching for more light. You can behead it, let the cut end dry for a few days, then set it on dry gritty compost to root. The old stump may also sprout new rosettes. Give it a much brighter spot from now on.
I've got way too many courgette seedlings. draft something to Kwame at the allotment offering a few?
Try: "Hi Kwame, I've ended up with far too many courgette seedlings. Would you like a few for your plot? They're strong little plants, just let me know and I'll bring them along."
peace lily is totally drooping, looks dead

Peace lilies dramatically flop when thirsty, and they usually perk up within hours of a proper drink. Water it thoroughly and let it drain. If the soil is already wet, though, suspect root rot and consider repotting into fresh compost.
kettle's got that white crust again, London water. quickest fix?

Fill it with equal parts water and white vinegar (or a spoonful of citric acid in water), bring it to the boil and leave it for about 20 minutes. Then rinse and boil fresh water once or twice to clear the taste.
washing machine has a musty smell now it's warmer

Wipe the rubber door seal and detergent drawer, where the grime usually builds up, and clean the filter if yours has one. Then run an empty hot cycle with a machine cleaner or a little white vinegar, and leave the door ajar between washes.
black spots on the bathroom sealant, how do I get rid

Spray it with a mould remover, leave it for the time on the label, then scrub gently and rinse. Keep the room ventilated and never mix bleach products with anything else. If the black goes right through the sealant, it's best to replace it.
sun cream has left yellowy marks on my white shirts
Rub washing-up liquid into the marks, since it cuts through the oils, and leave it for 15 minutes or so. Then wash as warm as the care label allows.
can I just use bleach?
I'd avoid chlorine bleach, as it can react with sun cream and make the stains darker. An oxygen-based stain remover soaked in warm water is safer and works well on whites.
dishwasher smells a bit off, filter maybe?
Very likely. Take out the filter at the bottom, rinse off the trapped gunk and scrub it under warm water. Then run an empty hot cycle with a dishwasher cleaner or a little citric acid in the bottom.
oven is grim and I don't want harsh chemicals in the flat

Make a paste of bicarbonate of soda and water, spread it on the inside surfaces, avoiding the heating elements, and leave it overnight. In the morning, wipe it out with a damp cloth and finish with a spray of diluted vinegar to lift the residue.
kitchen sink drain smells awful

It's usually trapped grease and food. Pour in hot water with a good squirt of washing-up liquid, then bicarbonate of soda followed by vinegar, leave it to fizz for a few minutes and flush with more hot water. Scrub the plug and overflow too, as they hold a lot of smell.
so much dust and pollen on my shelves lately. feather duster not helping
Feather dusters mostly just move it around. Use a slightly damp microfibre cloth so the dust sticks, work from top to bottom, and rinse or wash the cloth often so you aren't spreading it again.
fridge needs a proper clean. best way to do it without a faff?

Take everything out, bin anything past its date, and wash the shelves and drawers in warm water with a little washing-up liquid. Wipe the inside with a cloth wrung out in water and a spoonful of bicarbonate of soda, dry it all, and don't forget the door seals.
gym kit still smells even after washing

Skip fabric softener, since it traps odour in synthetic fabrics. Soak the kit for 30 minutes in water with a cup of white vinegar before a normal wash, and dry it fully and quickly, because damp is what brings the smell back.
wooden chopping board is stained and reeks of garlic

Sprinkle coarse salt over it and scrub with half a lemon, then rinse and leave it standing on its edge to dry fully. Once it's dry, a little food-safe mineral oil will stop it soaking up smells and stains.

AB test came back p=0.06, uplift 3%. Kwame says its a loss. is it?

Not necessarily. A p-value of 0.06 doesn't mean the variant lost. It means that if there were truly no difference, you'd see a result at least this extreme about 6% of the time. The 0.05 line is a convention, not a law of nature. It's also worth separating three outcomes: 'significant win', 'no evidence either way', and 'significant loss'. You're in the middle one, closer to the first than the third.

The confidence interval is more useful than the p-value here. If it runs from, say, -0.2% to +6.2%, the data are consistent with a small harm and a decent gain, and the test was probably underpowered for a 3% effect. Then the question is whether the change is cheap and low-risk to ship anyway, and whether running the test longer is worth the time. If you decide to extend it, fix the extra duration in advance. Stopping the moment p dips below 0.05 inflates your false positive rate.

Felix says overall conversion went up but its down in both mobile and desktop?? is the data broken

The data may well be fine. This is a known effect called Simpson's paradox. It happens when the mix of users shifts between groups that have different baseline rates.

Here's an illustration. Say desktop converts at 10% and mobile at 2%. Last month traffic was 30% desktop and 70% mobile, so overall conversion was about 4.4%. This month conversion fell to 9% on desktop and 1.8% on mobile, but traffic shifted to 60% desktop. The overall figure is then about 6.1%, higher than before even though both segments got worse.

So the headline number went up because more of your traffic comes from the high-converting segment, not because anything improved. To check, ask Felix for the traffic share by device in both periods. For decisions, the segment-level numbers are usually the better guide. You could also report a mix-adjusted figure that holds the traffic split constant.
monthly churn is 4%. Hugo put annual churn as 48% in his doc. right?

Not quite. Multiplying by 12 overstates it because churn compounds on a shrinking base. If 4% leave each month, 96% remain each month, so after a year you keep 0.96^12, which is about 61%. That makes annual churn roughly 39%, not 48%.

The 48% figure would only be right if you lost 4% of the original group every month and nobody else was counted, which isn't how a standard monthly rate works.

One caveat is that if the 4% is an average across customers of different ages, the true annual number can differ. New users usually churn faster than established ones, so the blended rate of an older base may be lower than the first-year figure. For Hugo's doc, simply state the formula, 1 - (1 - monthly rate)^12, and say whether it's a cohort or blended rate.
new homepage test was great week 1, flat by week 3. Ethan thinks the tracking is off. other explanation?

A very common explanation is a novelty effect. Returning users notice something new and click around more at first, then behave as they did before once it becomes familiar. The early lift fades as the novelty wears off.

The opposite exists too, a change aversion effect, where users initially dislike a change and recover later. Either way, short tests can mislead for features that existing users see repeatedly.

There are a few ways to check it. Split the results by new versus returning users. New users have no prior expectation, so their lift should be steadier if the change is truly better. Plot the daily effect, not just the cumulative result, to see the decay. Also check for seasonality, since a week-1 spike could coincide with a campaign or news event.

Tracking problems are still possible, but the pattern you describe fits novelty well. It's worth testing that before assuming the data is broken.
Nina asked whats a leading vs lagging indicator, with an example from our stuff. we're a note-sharing app

A lagging indicator tells you what has already happened. A leading indicator tells you something about what's likely to happen next, early enough that you can still act.

For a note-sharing app, 90-day retention is a classic lagging indicator. It's what you ultimately care about, but you only learn it three months after the users joined, so it's slow for steering. Paid conversion and churn are lagging for the same reason.

Leading candidates are early behaviours that correlate with staying. For example, 'shares a note with at least one other person in the first week' or 'invites a collaborator by day 3'. These show up within days, so you can respond quickly if they dip.

The important step is validating the link. Compare retention for users who did the behaviour with those who didn't, and be careful that it isn't just that engaged people do more of everything. A good leading indicator is one where moving it, through experiments, also moves the lagging outcome.

opportunity solution trees - what are they and are they worth it

An opportunity solution tree is a visual structure from Teresa Torres's continuous discovery approach. At the top is a desired outcome, such as "increase weekly active teams". Below it are customer opportunities, meaning needs, pain points or desires you've learned about from research. Under each opportunity are possible solutions, and under those are assumption tests.

Its value is that it links day-to-day work to an outcome and stops teams from jumping straight to a favourite solution. It makes gaps visible, for example when everything points at one opportunity. It also lets you compare several solutions for the same need rather than debating one idea.

It's worth it if you're doing regular customer interviews and need a shared picture of what you're learning. It's less useful if you have no ongoing research, since you'd be filling the tree with guesses. Keep it lightweight and revise it as you learn.
MoSCoW, quick rundown + the catch

MoSCoW is a prioritisation method that sorts requirements into four buckets for a given release or time box:

- Must have: without these the release fails or isn't viable.
- Should have: important, but there's a workaround or the release can still go ahead.
- Could have: nice to have if time allows, and first to go when things slip.
- Won't have (this time): explicitly agreed as out of scope for now.

It's quick and easy for stakeholders to grasp, which makes it good for aligning on scope. The catch is that everything tends to get labelled "Must", which defeats the purpose. A common guideline is to keep Musts to about 60% of the effort, so there's buffer for the rest. Another weakness is that it doesn't rank items within a bucket, and it says nothing about relative value or cost. The "Won't" list is the most useful part, because it records what you've agreed not to do.

Sketch still has a loyal following. It's a native Mac app, which some people find faster and more stable on very large files, and it works well offline. Some long-established teams also have mature libraries and plugins built around it, so switching has a real cost.

So the honest reasons to stay are inertia and strong offline or native-app preferences. If you're starting fresh or have a mixed-device team, Figma is the default choice.

my hollandaise just split, help

It's usually fixable. Take the pan off the heat right away so it stops cooking.

2. Add a spoonful of the split sauce and whisk hard until it comes together into a smooth emulsion.

how do I cook rice so it's not mushy. basmati

Here's a reliable absorption method for basmati:

1. Rinse the rice in a bowl or sieve under cold water, swirling, until the water runs mostly clear. This removes the surface starch that makes it gluey.
2. If you have time, soak it for 15 to 30 minutes and drain. This is optional.
3. Put it in a pan with a lid, add water at roughly 1.5 times the volume of rice (1.25 if you soaked it), and add a pinch of salt.
4. Bring to a boil, then turn the heat to its lowest, cover tightly and cook for 10 minutes.
5. Turn the heat off and leave it covered for 10 more minutes. Don't lift the lid during any of this.
6. Fluff with a fork.

The resting time matters a lot, because it lets the steam finish the job evenly.

1. Toast the nuts or seeds in a dry pan for a couple of minutes until golden, then let them cool.
2. Pulse them with a garlic clove and a pinch of salt until roughly chopped.

dal tadka, steps? red lentils

Dal tadka has two parts: a simple lentil base, then a spiced oil poured over at the end.

1. Rinse about a cup of red lentils until the water is clearer. Simmer them in around 3 cups of water with turmeric and a little salt for 15 to 20 minutes, skimming any foam, until they collapse into a soft porridge. Add water if it gets too thick.
2. While it cooks, soften a chopped onion in oil or ghee, then add grated ginger, garlic and a chopped tomato and cook until jammy. Stir this into the lentils.
3. For the tadka, heat ghee or oil in a small pan. Add cumin seeds, and when they sizzle, add a dried chilli, a pinch of asafoetida if you have it, and sliced garlic. Cook for under a minute until the garlic is golden.
4. Pour it straight over the dal, stir in lemon juice and fresh coriander, and serve with rice or flatbread.

Don't let the garlic burn, since it turns bitter very fast.

BoE moved 25 bps, what's a bps again? need to sound normal in standup

A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, so 100 basis points equal 1 percentage point. A 25 bps move is a quarter-point change, for example from 4.50% to 4.25%. Finance people use the unit because it avoids confusion between "a 1% rise" and "a 1 percentage point rise". Those are very different things when a rate is 4%. In standup you could say: "The Bank cut by 25 basis points, so a quarter of a point." If someone says "50 bps", that's half a point.
Need a one-liner on tech debt for Grace, she's non-technical and thinks it's just 'old stuff'

Here's one you could use: "Tech debt is the extra work we owe later because we took a shortcut now. Like borrowing against the future, we shipped faster, and now every new feature takes a bit longer because we're building on a shaky base." It's not the same as old software. Old systems that work fine and rarely change aren't really debt. The debt is in the places where the shortcuts make today's work slower or riskier. If she wants an analogy, try a kitchen where you never washed up between meals: it was quicker each time, but now cooking anything takes twice as long.
what actually is stagflation, people keep saying it like it's obvious

Stagflation is when an economy has weak or stagnant growth and high unemployment while inflation stays high at the same time. It's unusual because those normally move in opposite directions: slow economies tend to cool inflation. The classic case is the 1970s, when oil supply shocks pushed up costs everywhere while growth stalled. It's a nasty problem for central banks. Raising interest rates to fight inflation risks deepening the slowdown, and cutting rates to help growth risks feeding inflation. When people mention it today, they often mean "we might be heading that way" rather than that it's definitely happening.
explain opportunity cost simply. trying to argue we shouldn't take on the extra integration work

For your argument: "The integration looks small, but the real cost is the roadmap item the same two engineers would otherwise ship this quarter." That shifts the question from "is this worth doing?" to "is this worth more than the next best thing?" It helps to name the specific alternative so it doesn't sound abstract. Be ready for the counter that the integration might unlock something bigger, so have a view on its upside too.

latency vs throughput, the eng team keeps mixing them up in the doc and now so am I

Latency is how long a single request takes from start to finish, like the time for one page to load. Throughput is how many requests the system handles in a given period, like pages served per second. A useful picture is a motorway. Latency is how long one journey takes, and throughput is how many vehicles pass a point each minute. They're related but not the same. You can improve throughput by adding lanes without making any single journey faster. A system can also have low latency for one user and still fall over under heavy load. When reading the doc, ask "is this about one user's wait or about total volume?" and that usually settles which word belongs.
Lucia wrote "estoy aburrida" about the Monday catch-up and I thought it'd be ser. Why estar?

Both verbs are possible, but they mean different things. With aburrido/a, estar describes how someone feels: "Estoy aburrida" means "I'm bored." Ser describes a lasting quality of a person or thing: "Es aburrida" means "She is boring." Lucia is saying she's bored, so estar is correct. Several adjectives shift meaning the same way. "Es listo" means he's clever, while "está listo" means he's ready. "Es malo" means he's bad, and "está malo" means he's ill. A rough rule is ser for what something is like and estar for the state it's in right now.
is it "cuando era joven vivía en Madrid" or "viví"? Hugo used viví and I thought imperfect was the one for backstory

Both are grammatical, and the difference is in how you see the time. "Vivía en Madrid" treats it as background, a situation you were in with no stated end. It's the natural choice when you're setting a scene. "Viví en Madrid" treats it as a completed block of your life. It often comes with a span, as in "Viví en Madrid cuatro años." Hugo is probably framing it as a finished chapter. If a time limit is mentioned ("durante cuatro años", "hasta 2019"), the preterite is the safer choice. Without one, the imperfect sounds more like reminiscing.
why "cuando llegues" and not "cuando llegas"?

Spanish uses the subjunctive after cuando when the action hasn't happened yet. "Avísame cuando llegues" means "tell me when you arrive," and the arrival is still in the future and unconfirmed. The subjunctive marks that it's a anticipated event rather than a fact. The same pattern works with en cuanto, tan pronto como, hasta que and después de que. A quick check is to see whether the main clause points to the future or is a command. If it does, you probably need the subjunctive.
and if it's a habit? like "when I get in I always..."

Then it's the indicative, because the action is a real, repeated fact. "Cuando llego, siempre saludo a todos" is correct. The past works the same way: "Cuando llegué, ya habían empezado" uses the indicative because it actually happened.
why "el agua fría" and not "la agua fría"? agua is feminine right?

You're right that agua is feminine. The adjective proves it, since it's "fría" and not "frío." The article changes to "el" only for pronunciation. Feminine nouns that begin with a stressed "a" sound would produce an awkward "la agua," so Spanish uses "el" in the singular. The same applies to el águila, el hacha and el alma. In the plural the normal article returns: "las aguas frías." The article also goes back to "la" if something sits between it and the noun, as in "la misma agua" or "la otra águila" (though usage varies). A good habit is to treat these as feminine nouns with a special singular article.
"le envié el informe a Grace" → why does it become "se lo envié" and not "le lo envié"?

Spanish avoids "le lo" and "les lo," so when an indirect object pronoun (le or les) comes right before a direct object pronoun beginning with l (lo, la, los, las), it changes to se. That gives "Le envié el informe a Grace" becoming "Se lo envié." Here "lo" stands for "el informe" and "se" stands for Grace. This se has nothing to do with the reflexive se, even though it looks the same. The indirect pronoun always goes first. With other persons nothing changes, so you still say "Me lo envió" and "Te lo envié." Because se is ambiguous, speakers often add "a Grace" or "a ellos" for clarity.

The verb agrees with the thing that pleases, "las reuniones cortas," which is plural, so it's gustan. The person who likes is the indirect object, me. With a singular thing or an infinitive, it's singular: "Me gusta el formato" and "Me gusta trabajar en equipo." The same structure applies to encantar, interesar, molestar, importar and parecer.

when do tu/si/mas get accents again

The accent separates words that are spelled the same but do different jobs. The main pairs are:
- tú (you) vs tu (your): "Tú tienes tu informe."
- sí (yes, or reflexive "itself") vs si (if): "Sí, si puedo, voy."
- más (more) vs mas (but, rare and literary)
- él (he) vs el (the)
- mí (me, after a preposition) vs mi (my): "Es para mí, no para mi jefe."
- té (tea) vs te (you, as object): "Te traigo un té."
- sé (I know, or imperative of ser) vs se (reflexive or impersonal): "Yo sé que se fue."
The accented form is usually the one that stands alone and carries meaning, while the unaccented one is a small connecting word.
saber or conocer for "I know Alice" and "I know the answer"?

The personal a appears before Alice because she's a specific person. Saber means to know a fact or a piece of information, or how to do something: "Sé la respuesta" and "Sabe programar." kettle's got that white crust inside, how do I get rid of it without scrubbing forever

self review para, be honest: "I was involved in the onboarding redesign and helped with user research. I also supported the engineers during build and was part of the launch discussions."

Honestly, it undersells you. "Involved in," "helped with," "supported" and "part of" all describe presence rather than contribution, so a reviewer can't tell what you actually did. Use verbs that show ownership, such as led, decided, defined, unblocked or negotiated. Then add the result for each one. For example: "I led product on the onboarding redesign, running eight user interviews that shaped the new three-step flow. During build I made the scope calls that kept us on schedule, and I set the launch criteria. Completion of onboarding rose from [X]% to [Y]%." research summary para: "Users generally found the dashboard confusing and said it was hard to find things. Many were frustrated. Overall the experience needs improvement."

The conclusion is probably right, but nobody reading this can act on it. "Generally," "many" and "confusing" don't say how widespread the problem is, where it happens or what it looked like. Add the sample size, the specific failure and a verbatim line from a participant. For example: "Six of the eight participants couldn't find the export button within a minute, and four opened the settings menu first. One said, 'I assumed it would be somewhere under my account.'" RICE gives each idea a score from four inputs: Reach, Impact, Confidence and Effort. The formula is (Reach × Impact × Confidence) ÷ Effort. Reach is how many people the change touches in a set period, for example 2,000 users per quarter. Impact is usually scored on a fixed scale: 3 for massive, 2 for high, 1 for medium, 0.5 for low and 0.25 for minimal. Confidence is a percentage showing how much evidence you have, so 100% means solid data, 80% means some, and 50% means mostly a hunch. Effort is total person-months across product, design and engineering. Higher scores float to the top, but treat the output as a conversation starter rather than a verdict. Scores can look more precise than they are, so if something ranks oddly, ask which input is shaky before you override the number.

Jobs to be done says people don't buy products for their attributes. They "hire" them to make progress in a particular situation. The usual format is: "When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [outcome]." For example: "When I'm running late for a meeting, I want to tell attendees quickly, so I don't look unprofessional." That's different from a persona. exchange.text: Grace asked why our north star can't just be revenue. what do I say

A good answer is that revenue is a result of customers getting value, not a measure of whether they're getting it. A North Star metric should capture the core value customers receive, and revenue is a lagging indicator that moves slowly and can be pushed up in ways that hurt the product. Airbnb's "nights booked" is a common example. It reflects value for guests and hosts and leads to revenue, and teams can influence it directly. A solid North Star passes three tests. It reflects real customer value, it predicts long-term business health, and teams can move it through their daily work. Revenue fails the third test, because most of a team's decisions can't be traced to it. You'd still track it, but as a business outcome alongside the North Star. Beneath the North Star you'd also break out a handful of input metrics, such as activation or frequency, which individual teams own.

exchange.text: stakeholders think everything is a must. how does MoSCoW stop that

MoSCoW sorts scope into Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have (this time). It only works if you give "Must" a hard definition. A good test is that if the item is missing, the release is unsafe, unusable or pointless. Everything else is a Should or lower, however much someone wants it. A common guardrail is to keep Musts to about 60% of the total effort. That leaves room for Shoulds and Coulds to absorb surprises without missing the date. The "Won't" column matters as much as the others. It records what you've deliberately parked, which cuts down on repeat requests. When someone insists their item is a Must, ask what specifically breaks without it and who is affected. If they can't answer, it moves down.
kano model - what is it and when is it useful

The Kano model sorts features by how they affect satisfaction. Basic expectations, like the app not crashing, only cause dissatisfaction when missing and earn no praise when present. Performance features, such as speed, bring satisfaction in proportion to how well you do them. Delighters are unexpected extras that give a big boost but cause no complaints when absent. There are also indifferent features that people don't care about. Delighters tend to become expectations over time, so what wowed users three years ago may be a basic requirement now. You find out which category a feature falls in by asking two survey questions per feature: how would you feel if it were present, and how would you feel if it were absent. It's most useful when you're deciding where to invest beyond table stakes, or explaining why fixing lots of small things isn't producing excitement.

The delivery track builds and ships what discovery has validated. They aren't separate departments, and the same product manager, designer and engineers take part in both. Discovery usually stays a sprint or two ahead, so delivery always has validated work ready. The main benefit is that you stop putting unproven ideas into sprints just to keep engineers busy. The most common failure is turning it into a handoff, where one group researches and another builds without context. In Shape Up, which is Basecamp's method, appetite is how much time you're willing to spend on a problem, decided before the work starts. That's the reverse of the usual practice of estimating how long something will take. A typical appetite is a small batch of one or two weeks, or a big batch of a full six-week cycle. Time is fixed and scope is variable. The team shapes a solution that fits the appetite, and if it gets harder than expected, they cut scope rather than extend the deadline. exchange.text: how do you actually know if you have product-market fit? everyone says 'you'll feel it'

Feelings are unreliable, so here are some more concrete signals. The best-known is the Sean Ellis test. You ask users how they'd feel if they could no longer use the product, and if 40% or more say "very disappointed," that's a strong sign. The second is retention. Plot the percentage of each cohort still active over time, and if the curve flattens rather than sliding to zero, you've got a group who keeps getting value. The third is qualitative, meaning unprompted word of mouth, customers pulling the product into new uses, and demand that outpaces your ability to serve it. None of these is conclusive on its own, and the 40% figure is a rule of thumb rather than a law. Fit can also be narrow, so check whether it holds for a specific segment even if the overall numbers look mediocre. That's often where to focus first.
WSJF / cost of delay - what's the idea? Oscar threw it out in planning

WSJF stands for Weighted Shortest Job First, a prioritisation method from SAFe. It's based on cost of delay, meaning how much value you lose for each unit of time an item isn't delivered. The formula is Cost of Delay ÷ Job Duration (or size). So a small item with a moderate cost of delay can outrank a huge item with a high one, because you capture value sooner. Cost of delay is typically scored relatively, often with Fibonacci numbers, from three parts: user or business value, time criticality (is there a deadline or a window that closes?), and risk reduction or opportunity enablement. You score each item against the others rather than in absolute terms. It's particularly good at surfacing time-sensitive work that a plain value ranking would bury. As with RICE, it only helps if the scores come from a group discussion rather than one person's guess.
Google HEART framework, what are the letters and how do I use it for a new search feature

HEART stands for Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention and Task success. It's a set of user-centred categories for choosing metrics, and you pair it with a Goals-Signals-Metrics process. For each category, ask what the goal is, what behaviour would signal it, and which metric captures that. For a new search feature it could look like this:
- Happiness: goal is that people find search satisfying. Metric is a satisfaction rating after a search, or the share of searches followed by a thumbs-up.
- Engagement: goal is regular use. Metric is searches per active user per week.
- Adoption: goal is that new users try it. Metric is the percentage of users who run a search in their first week.
- Retention: goal is that people keep using it. Metric is the share of searchers who search again within 30 days.
- Task success: goal is that people find what they want. Metric is the click-through rate on results and the share of searches that don't end in a reformulation.
You don't need all five for every project, so pick the two or three that match what you're trying to learn.
Kwame wants to run a pre-mortem before launch. how does that work, what's the format

A pre-mortem asks the team to imagine the launch has already failed and then work out why. Because the failure is treated as a fact, people find it easier to raise worries they'd otherwise keep quiet. A simple 45-minute format works like this:
1. Set the scene (5 min): "It's three months after launch and it went badly. What happened?"
2. Silent writing (10 min): everyone writes their own reasons for failure on separate notes, without discussing, so louder voices don't dominate.
3. Share and cluster (10 min): read them out, group similar ones, and look for themes.
4. Vote (5 min): each person marks the risks they think are most likely or most damaging.
5. Plan (15 min): for the top risks, decide on a mitigation, an owner, and an early warning sign to watch for.
Include people from engineering, support and marketing as well as product, since they tend to see different risks. Afterwards, share the outcomes with the wider team so the actions get followed up.

whats the actual difference between activation and retention? Imogen keeps using them interchangeably in standup

They measure different moments. Activation is whether a new user reaches the first point where they get real value, often called the aha moment. Examples are sending their first message, creating their first project, or connecting a data source. It's usually measured within a short window after signup, such as 'percent of new users who do X within 7 days'.

Retention is whether users keep coming back and repeating valuable behaviour over time. It's usually shown as the share of a cohort still active on day 7, day 30, week 12 and so on.

Activation comes first and is a leading indicator for retention. If people never activate, there's nothing to retain. Interchangeable use causes real problems, because a fix for weak activation (onboarding, setup friction) is very different from a fix for weak retention (habit loops, ongoing value, re-engagement). It's worth asking Imogen which behaviour and which time window she means each time the word comes up.
why does everyone obsess over cohort retention curves instead of just overall active users

Overall active user counts blend together people who joined at very different times, so they can hide what's happening. If you're adding lots of new users, the total can rise even while every group of users is leaving faster than before. Growth masks leakage.

A cohort curve follows one group, for example everyone who signed up in the week of 2 June, and shows what share are still active after 1, 2, 3 weeks and so on. That lets you compare like with like. You can see whether June signups stick better than March signups, and whether a product change actually improved things.

The shape matters too. A curve that drops and then flattens means you've found a core of users who stay, and the flat level is roughly your long-term retention. A curve that keeps sliding toward zero suggests there's no durable habit yet. That distinction is hard to see in a single total.
explain north star metric like I'm new, Freya's joining the team and asked

Here's a version you could give Freya, as plain as I can make it:

A North Star metric is the single number that best captures whether customers are getting real value from the product. When it goes up in a healthy way, the business should do well over time. It's meant to keep teams pointed in the same direction.

A good one has three traits. It reflects value delivered to the customer, not just activity on our side. It's a leading indicator of long-term success. And teams can actually influence it through their work. 'Weekly active teams completing a shared task' is a better example than 'page views', because page views can rise without anyone getting value.

It works best alongside a few supporting inputs, such as activation, frequency and breadth of use, that individual teams own. It also shouldn't stand alone. You'd pair it with guardrails so nobody pushes it up at the expense of quality.
DAU/MAU of 18%, is that bad?

It depends heavily on what the product is for. DAU/MAU, often called stickiness, tells you roughly what fraction of your monthly users show up on a given day. 18% means the average monthly user is active about 5 days a month.

For a product built for daily habits, such as messaging or a social feed, that would be weak. Strong ones sit well above 50%. For a tool people naturally use weekly or a few times a month, like planning, reporting or admin software, 15-25% can be perfectly healthy.

So the useful question is what frequency the product should have. If the real use case is weekly, then WAU/MAU is the fairer measure. Also look at the trend and at segments. A flat 18% with power users at 60% and a long tail at 3% tells a very different story from a uniform 18%.

SRM is sample ratio mismatch. It means the number of users in each arm differs from the planned split by more than chance would explain. With 200k users, a 52/48 split is a meaningful gap. Expected random variation at that size is only around 0.1 to 0.2 percentage points. So Dmitri is probably right, and a chi-squared test on the counts would confirm it.

It matters because SRM usually signals a bug in assignment or tracking, not bad luck. Typical causes are one variant loading slower so more users bounce before being logged, bot filtering applied unevenly, a redirect that drops some users, or events firing differently between arms.

Once SRM is present, the results are unreliable even if they look great, since the users you lost are probably not random. Don't panic, but don't ship on this result. Find the cause, fix it and rerun.

Typical guardrails include performance and error rates, unsubscribe or complaint rates, customer support volume, and downstream retention. A north star metric is the single number that best captures the value customers get from your product, and that you expect to drive long-term growth. A good one has a few traits:

- It reflects delivered value, not just activity. "Weekly active users" is weaker than "weekly teams completing a shared project".

- Teams can influence it through their daily work.

The usual practice is to pair it with 3 to 5 input metrics, such as activation rate, frequency of use and breadth of adoption. Those are what individual teams own. Felix wants to use RICE for the backlog. remind me how it works and where it goes wrong

RICE scores each item as (Reach × Impact × Confidence) ÷ Effort.

- Reach: how many users or events are affected in a set period, for example per quarter.
- Impact: a rough scale, often 3 = massive, 2 = high, 1 = medium, 0.5 = low, 0.25 = minimal.
- Confidence: a percentage reflecting how much evidence you have behind your estimates.
- Effort: usually person-months.

It works well for forcing explicit assumptions and for comparing a long list of similar-sized ideas. It goes wrong when the numbers get treated as precise. Impact is mostly guesswork, and teams often adjust inputs until their favourite wins. It also undervalues strategic bets, foundational work and anything with hard-to-measure reach. Treat the score as a conversation starter, not a verdict.

explain jobs to be done like I'm presenting it to the team in 2 mins

Jobs to be done is the idea that people don't buy products for their demographics, they "hire" them to make progress in a particular situation. The classic example is the milkshake that commuters hired to make a boring drive more interesting and keep them full until lunch. That's a different job from the one parents had in mind when they bought it for a treat.

A job is usually framed as: "When I'm in [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [outcome]." It has functional, emotional and social dimensions. Your real competition is whatever else gets hired for the job, which might be a spreadsheet, a colleague or doing nothing.

In practice, you learn the jobs by interviewing recent customers about what led them to switch, what they tried before and what nearly stopped them. Those stories shape positioning, onboarding and roadmap priorities. The big benefit is that it shifts the team from "what features do users ask for?" to "what progress are they trying to make?"

exchange.text: kano model, what's the gist

The Kano model sorts features by how they affect satisfaction, to show that not all improvements are equal.

- Must-haves (basic expectations): customers barely notice them when present but are very unhappy when they're missing, like reliable login.
- Performance features: more is better, and satisfaction rises roughly in line with them, such as speed or storage.
- Delighters: unexpected touches that create a strong positive reaction, though no one misses them when absent.
- Indifferent and reverse features: some changes don't matter, and some actively annoy a segment of users.

It's typically researched with paired survey questions: how would you feel if the feature were present, and how if it were absent. One important dynamic is that delighters drift into must-haves over time as expectations rise. It's best for deciding what mix of features a release needs, not for ranking individual items precisely.
Grace asked what dual-track agile actually means. short version?

Dual-track agile runs two connected streams of work at the same time: discovery and delivery.

Discovery is about working out what's worth building. It includes customer interviews, prototypes, assumption tests and feasibility checks, usually done by the product manager, designer and an engineer together. Delivery is about building and shipping validated work in the normal sprint or flow cadence.

The point is that ideas are tested cheaply before they consume engineering capacity, and delivery always has a pipeline of well-understood work. They're not separate teams or phases. The same people often straddle both, and discovery runs ahead of delivery by a sprint or two. The usual pitfall is letting discovery become a handoff stage, where the product manager researches alone and then "throws specs over the wall".
