exchange.text: feature flags — benefits and risks, brief

Feature flags are switches in the code that let you turn functionality on or off without redeploying.

Benefits:
- You can separate deploying code from releasing it to users.
- Progressive rollouts let you expose a feature to 1%, then 10%, then everyone, while watching for problems.
- A faulty feature can be switched off in seconds instead of rolling back a release.
- They enable beta groups, internal dogfooding and A/B experiments.

Risks:
- Old flags pile up and become clutter, so you need a clean-up habit.
- Combinations of flags multiply the states your product can be in, which makes testing harder.
- Unclear ownership means nobody knows whether a flag is safe to remove.

A good practice is to give every flag an owner, a purpose and an expected removal date at creation.
NPS vs CSAT, when do you use which

They measure different things.

CSAT (customer satisfaction) asks how satisfied someone was with a specific interaction or feature, usually on a 1 to 5 scale. It's best right after an event, like a support chat or a completed checkout, because it tells you how that moment went.

NPS (Net Promoter Score) asks how likely someone is to recommend you on a 0 to 10 scale. Scores of 9 to 10 are promoters, 7 to 8 are passives and 0 to 6 are detractors. NPS is calculated as promoters minus detractors, as a percentage. It's a broader measure of overall relationship and loyalty, so it's better asked periodically than after each interaction.

Use CSAT to diagnose particular touchpoints and NPS to track sentiment over time. Neither is very useful alone, so read the open-text follow-up answers, which is where the actionable detail sits. Also compare NPS with your own history and segments, since benchmarks across industries and cultures vary a lot.
what is product-led growth, proper definition, not buzzwords

Product-led growth (PLG) is a go-to-market approach where the product itself is the main driver of acquiring, converting and expanding customers. Rather than relying on sales conversations to show value, users experience it directly, often through a free tier, free trial or self-serve sign-up.

Typical features include a low-friction start, a fast route to a first moment of value (often called the "aha moment"), and built-in sharing or collaboration that pulls in more users. Upgrades happen when people hit usage limits or need more advanced capabilities. Tools like Slack, Dropbox and Figma are the usual examples.

It's not "no sales". Many PLG companies add a sales team later to handle larger organisations, sometimes called product-led sales. It works best when the product is easy to adopt without a lot of setup and value shows up quickly for an individual user. It works less well for complex products that need heavy integration before anything useful happens.
A/B testing pitfalls? Imogen's about to run her first one

The common ones are worth sharing with her up front:

1. Peeking: checking results daily and stopping when it looks significant inflates false positives. Decide the sample size and duration beforehand, or use a method designed for sequential testing.
2. Underpowered tests: too little traffic means you can't detect realistic effects. Estimate the minimum detectable effect and the needed sample size before starting.
3. Too many metrics: if you look at twenty, one will look significant by chance. Choose one primary metric and a few guardrail metrics in advance.
4. Ending mid-cycle: run for at least one or two full weeks so weekday and weekend behaviour are both covered.
5. Uneven assignment: check the groups are split as intended, since a mismatch usually signals a bug.
6. Novelty effects: a change can win simply because it's new, so be cautious with short tests.

Also write down the hypothesis and the decision rule before launch.
what's a guardrail metric again

It's a metric you don't want to harm while improving the primary one, such as page load time, unsubscribe rate or support contacts. If the primary metric rises but a guardrail drops noticeably, the result is suspect.
cohort retention curves, how do I read them

A cohort retention analysis groups users by when they started, for example the week they signed up. It then tracks what share of each group is still active in later periods. You usually see it as a triangle table or as one line per cohort.

What to look for:
- Shape: a curve that drops and then flattens suggests a core of users who find lasting value. One that keeps falling towards zero suggests the product isn't sticking.
- Where the cliff is: a steep drop in week one points at onboarding or activation problems.
- Trend across cohorts: if newer cohorts sit above older ones, your changes are probably helping.
- Definition of "active": make sure it means a meaningful action, not just opening the app.

Cohorts avoid the misleading effect of blended averages, where a surge of new sign-ups can mask poor retention among older users. Be careful with small cohorts, since the percentages bounce around.
what's a PR/FAQ, the Amazon thing

A PR/FAQ is a document from Amazon's "working backwards" approach. You write the internal press release and FAQ for a product as if it were launching, before building anything.

The press release is usually one page. It has a headline, a summary, the customer problem, how the product solves it, a quote from a team leader and a quote from a hypothetical customer. The FAQ has two parts: external questions customers would ask, and internal ones about feasibility, risks, dependencies and metrics.

The discipline is that it forces clarity about who the customer is and why they'd care, in plain language. If the press release sounds dull or confusing, the idea probably needs work. It also surfaces hard questions early, when changing course is cheap. Teams typically review it together and rewrite it many times, and it's often a short narrative rather than a polished marketing piece.
tips for customer interviews? Kwame's doing his first ones next week

A few principles that make a big difference:

- Ask about past behaviour, not hypotheticals. "Tell me about the last time you did X" gives better evidence than "Would you use a feature that does X?"
- Avoid leading questions and don't pitch your idea. People tend to be polite and say it sounds great.
- Dig into specifics with follow-ups like "What happened next?" and "Why was that hard?"
- Listen for workarounds, since they signal real pain.
- Stay quiet after an answer, because people often fill the silence with the useful part.
- Talk to people who recently did the thing, so their memory is fresh.
- Take notes or record with permission, and capture quotes rather than interpretations.

Aim for patterns across five to ten interviews in a segment rather than treating any single comment as truth. Debrief soon after each one, while details are still fresh.
Slack or Teams for a 40-person company? Half the team lives in Outlook already

If most of the team already lives in Outlook and Microsoft 365, Teams is usually the lower-friction choice. Chat, video calls, file sharing and SharePoint storage come as one package, and sign-in is handled by the accounts people already have. Slack is generally nicer for day-to-day chat. Channels are easier to browse, search is better, and the third-party integrations are more polished. It also tends to win on culture, since people actually enjoy using it. The tradeoff is that you'd be running a second tool next to Microsoft's, and video calls would still need a separate home or Slack Huddles.

At 40 people the decision is mostly about habits, not features. If you have a lot of engineers or tools like GitHub and PagerDuty feeding alerts into chat, Slack's ecosystem matters more. If the team is mostly ops, sales and admin and already in Outlook, Teams will cause less resistance. Either way, the worst outcome is running both with no clear rule about which is for what.
Jira vs Linear for a team of 8 devs, 2 designers. We're currently drowning in Jira config

For a team that size, and with that complaint, Linear is probably the better fit. It's opinionated and fast. Cycles, projects and roadmaps work out of the box, and there's very little admin to maintain. Keyboard shortcuts and the GitHub integration make it pleasant for developers, which tends to improve how well tickets actually get updated.

Jira's strength is flexibility: custom workflows, fields, permissions, and reporting that scales to hundreds of people and multiple teams. That same flexibility is what causes the config sprawl you're describing. If you don't need that depth, you're paying the complexity cost for nothing.

The main reasons to stay on Jira would be heavy dependence on Confluence, specific compliance or audit needs, or a plan to grow a lot with several teams needing very different workflows. Otherwise, trial Linear with one team for a cycle or two before deciding. Migration is usually manageable at your size, though you'd want to decide what history is worth bringing across.
notion or confluence for our product docs? need something people will actually keep updated

For getting people to keep docs updated, Notion usually wins. Creating and editing pages is quick and flexible, and databases let you link specs, decisions and projects in a way that feels natural. That lowers the effort of writing things down, which is the main driver of whether docs stay current.

Confluence is stronger if you're already in Jira, since the linking between tickets and pages is tight. It also has more mature permissions, page-level controls and admin features, which matter in larger or more regulated organisations. The downside is that it can feel heavier, and spaces tend to turn into graveyards without active gardening.

Whichever you choose, what keeps docs alive is ownership. Give each area a named owner, use a simple template for specs, and add a last-reviewed date near the top of each page. A tool with less friction helps, but those habits matter more.
Zoom or Google Meet for calls with external clients?

Both are fine, so it comes down to what your clients are comfortable with. Zoom is the more familiar name outside tech, and its connection quality is generally strong on weaker networks. It also has good breakout rooms, polished recording, and a client that most people have already used. Meet is simpler: it runs in the browser with no install, and joining via a link is very smooth if people use Google accounts. It's tightly integrated with Gmail and Google Calendar.

For external calls, the biggest factor is usually the friction of joining. Some clients' IT policies block certain tools, so it's worth asking what they prefer. If they have no preference and your team is on Google Workspace, Meet is enough. If you run webinars or larger sessions, or want the more feature-rich option, Zoom is the safer pick.
they're a bank so probably locked down

In that case, ask them which they allow before choosing. Banks often have an approved tool, and it's frequently Teams or sometimes Zoom, with Meet less commonly whitelisted. Using whatever they already support will avoid a messy first call.
Miro vs FigJam for workshops. we use Figma already

Since you already use Figma, FigJam is an easy default. It's in the same workspace, your team already has accounts, and you can drop in designs or components directly. It's also lighter and friendlier for quick brainstorms, with stickers, stamps, voting and simple templates that make sessions feel playful.

Miro is the more powerful whiteboard. It has a bigger template library, better tools for large or structured boards like journey maps and story maps, more integrations, and stronger facilitation features such as timers, private mode and presentation tools. It tends to cope better with very large, complicated boards and bigger groups.

For typical product workshops with a handful of people, FigJam will do the job and saves you adding another tool. If you regularly run big, multi-team sessions or need heavier facilitation features, Miro is worth the extra tool.
Loom vs just recording on Teams for async product updates?

For async updates, Loom is usually the better experience. Recording takes a click, the video is instantly shareable by link, and viewers can watch at faster speeds, comment at specific timestamps and react. It also captures your face in a small bubble over the screen, which people tend to like. Transcripts and chapters help people skim.

Recording in Teams works but is clunkier. It's designed around meetings, so you'd start a meeting alone, record, and wait for processing before it appears in SharePoint or OneDrive. Permissions can also be fiddly if you share beyond your organisation.

If your company is strict about using only Microsoft tools, Teams recording, or Clipchamp and Stream, is the safe choice. Otherwise, Loom is worth it for regular updates, and keeping each video under about five minutes with a short written summary underneath makes them far more likely to be watched.
Productboard vs Aha for roadmapping. Not sure which suits a 15-person product org

They lean in different directions. Productboard is built around capturing customer feedback and tying it to features, so it suits teams that want evidence of what customers ask for to drive prioritisation. Its insights inbox, scoring and portal features support that, and the roadmap views are easy to share.

Aha is more of an end-to-end strategy and planning tool. It covers goals, initiatives, release planning and detailed roadmap views, and it has strong customisation and reporting. It can feel heavier and more structured, which works well if you need to link strategy to delivery and report upward.

For 15 people, a useful question is whether your main pain is making sense of feedback or aligning plans to goals. If it's feedback, I'd lean Productboard. If it's strategic structure and reporting, Aha. It's also worth asking whether a lighter option, such as Linear's roadmaps or a well-built Notion database, would cover your needs before committing.
Asana or Trello for a marketing team of 6 who hate process

Trello is probably the better match for people who dislike process. A board with cards and columns is understood within minutes, and there's almost nothing to configure. It suits campaign pipelines, content calendars and simple stage-based work. Power-Ups add things like calendar views and automation when needed.

Asana offers more structure: dependencies, timelines, workload views, forms and reporting across projects. That's useful as work gets more complicated, with multiple campaigns, deadlines that depend on each other and several stakeholders. But for a team that resists process, extra fields and views can feel like admin, and adoption may drop.

I'd start with Trello and agree a small set of columns, such as Ideas, In progress, In review and Done. If you find yourselves needing dependencies or cross-project visibility, that's the signal to move to Asana.

This is the most common half marathon mistake, and it can be fixed with a plan. Aim to run the first 3 to 5k about 5 to 10 seconds per km slower than your goal pace, even though it will feel almost too easy. Adrenaline and the crowd will push you to surge, so check your watch regularly early on and hold back. From around 5k to 15k, settle onto goal pace and stay relaxed, focusing on steady breathing and shoulders loose. It covers your instructions, the conversation so far, any documents you paste in, and the answer it's writing. It's measured in tokens, which are chunks of words, roughly three-quarters of an English word each. If a conversation or document goes past the limit, the model can't take in the extra part, so older content has to be cut or summarised. A bigger window lets you work with longer documents. It doesn't guarantee the model uses everything in it equally well, though, and details in the middle of very long inputs can get missed. The 3:1 rule of thumb says a customer should be worth about three times what it cost to acquire them. Below that, growth may not pay off. Much higher, say 6:1 or more, can mean you're under-investing in growth. It's only a heuristic, though. It depends on how long it takes to earn back the acquisition cost (the payback period), your margins, and how reliable your churn estimate is. The practical version has two flavours. Direct effects come from users connecting with each other. Indirect or two-sided effects come from groups attracting each other, like more sellers drawing in buyers and vice versa. The consequences are a hard cold-start problem, because early on there's little value, and a strong lead for whoever gets big first. A common mistake is calling something a network effect when it's just scale economies or a popular brand. The test is whether an extra user makes the product better for the existing ones.

exchange.text: CDN vs edge computing? are they the same thing

They're related but not the same. A CDN, or content delivery network, stores copies of your content, such as images, videos and scripts, on servers around the world so users get it from a nearby location. That makes pages load faster and reduces strain on your main servers. Edge computing goes further by running actual logic on those nearby servers, not just storing files. For example, it could personalise a page or check a request close to the user. Many CDN providers now offer edge computing as well, which is why the terms get blurred. A simple way to remember: a CDN is about delivering content closer to people, and edge computing is about doing processing closer to them.

It doesn't tell you the probability that B is better. That would need a different kind of analysis, such as a Bayesian approach with assumptions about what you expected beforehand. A p-value below 0.05 is the usual threshold for calling a result statistically significant, so 0.03 is a reasonable signal. Still, check the sample size, whether you looked at the results repeatedly and stopped early, and how big the effect is in practice. Significant doesn't always mean important.

exchange.text: explain "si tuviera tiempo, lo haría" - why those two forms

This is the standard pattern for hypothetical, unlikely or contrary-to-fact situations. The si clause takes the imperfect subjunctive (tuviera), and the result clause takes the conditional (haría). It matches the English "If I had time, I would do it." The imperfect subjunctive has two forms, -ra (tuviera) and -se (tuviese), and they are usually interchangeable. A common error, even among native speakers, is to put the conditional in both clauses, as in "si tendría tiempo." That is considered incorrect. For a realistic possibility you use a different pattern, present indicative plus future: "Si tengo tiempo, lo haré."
"llevo dos años estudiando español" vs "hace dos años que estudio" - same thing?

They mean the same thing, which is that you started two years ago and are still studying. Both use the present tense for something that began in the past and continues now, which English handles with "I've been studying for two years." The structures are:
- Llevo + time + gerund: "Llevo dos años estudiando español."
- Hace + time + que + present: "Hace dos años que estudio español."
- Present + desde hace + time: "Estudio español desde hace dos años."
All three are natural, and llevo is probably the most common in speech. Be careful not to use the present perfect ("he estudiado") for this, since it doesn't convey that the activity is ongoing.
laptop fan is screaming and it's barely doing anything. mac

Start with Activity Monitor (Cmd+Space, type its name) and click the CPU tab, then sort by % CPU. A runaway browser tab, a video call app left open, or a stuck background process is the usual cause. Quit or force-quit whatever is at the top. If nothing stands out, restart the Mac, because that clears most odd background loads. It also helps to keep the laptop on a hard, flat surface, since a sofa or duvet blocks the vents and traps heat, especially in warm June weather. Check that your macOS is up to date as well, since updates sometimes fix fan and thermal bugs. If the fan is still loud after all that on a cold, idle machine, it may be clogged with dust and worth getting checked.
it was a zoom thing still running in the background lol

That's a classic. Zoom and similar apps can keep the camera or screen-sharing process running after a call ends. Fully quitting the app with Cmd+Q, rather than just closing the window, usually stops it.
bathroom ceiling has little black spots starting. what do I do

That's most likely mould from condensation, and it's easy to deal with if you catch it early. Mix a spray of water with a little washing-up liquid, or use a ready-made mould remover, and wipe the spots with a cloth. Rinse and dry the area properly afterwards. Wear gloves and open a door for airflow while you clean, and don't mix bleach with other cleaners. To stop it coming back, run the extractor fan during showers and for about 20 minutes afterwards. Wipe down wet surfaces and keep the bathroom door shut while you shower so steam doesn't spread to cooler rooms. If the spots keep returning or cover a large area, there may be a ventilation or damp issue that needs a proper look.
kitchen sink is draining super slowly. no plunger. help

Try the no-tool route first. Pour a kettle of just-boiled water down the drain to loosen grease. If your pipes are plastic, use very hot tap water rather than fully boiling. Then add about half a cup of baking soda, follow with half a cup of white vinegar, and leave it fizzing for 15 to 20 minutes. Flush with more hot water afterwards. If it's still slow, put a bucket under the U-bend beneath the sink, unscrew the two collars by hand, and clear out the gunk inside, which is often the real blockage. Reassemble it and run the tap to check for leaks. For next time, wipe greasy pans with kitchen paper before washing them, and use a sink strainer.
how do I get two apps side by side on my mac without resizing them manually

macOS has a built-in way to do it. Hover your mouse over the green button at the top left of a window, or click and hold it, and choose "Tile Window to Left of Screen" or "Right". Then pick the other app from the other half of the screen. Both windows will snap into place. On newer macOS versions you can also drag a window to the screen edge to tile it. To exit, hover over the green button again and choose to exit full screen, or press Esc. If you want more control over layouts, free tools like Rectangle let you use keyboard shortcuts to snap windows to halves, thirds and corners.
bathroom tap drips constantly and it's driving me mad. can I fix it myself

Often, yes. A dripping tap is usually a worn washer or cartridge. First turn off the water to that tap. Look for a small isolation valve on the pipe below the basin and turn it with a flat screwdriver. If there isn't one, you'll have to turn off the water at the main stopcock. Open the tap to drain what's left, and plug the basin so no small parts fall down the drain. Prise off the cap on the handle, unscrew the handle, and use a spanner to remove the part underneath. If it's a traditional tap, replace the rubber washer. If it's a ceramic disc type, replace the whole cartridge. Take the old part to a hardware shop so you get the right match. Reassemble, turn the water back on slowly, and check for leaks.
showerhead is crusty and the spray's gone wonky. quick fix?

Limescale is almost certainly blocking the nozzles, and vinegar will dissolve it. If the showerhead unscrews easily, remove it and soak it in a bowl of white vinegar for an hour or two. If it doesn't, fill a plastic bag with vinegar, pull it up over the showerhead and fasten it with a rubber band or hair tie so the head is fully submerged. Leave it for 1 to 2 hours. Don't do this with brass, gold-plated or natural stone fittings, as vinegar can damage them, and check the manufacturer's advice if you're unsure. Afterwards, remove the bag, rub the nozzles with an old toothbrush, and run the shower hot for a minute to flush out any loosened bits.
Grace wants to run a hackathon day in June. theme ideas? needs to be relevant to product folks not just engineers

Themes that give non-engineers a way in tend to be about problems, not technologies. Here are some options:

1. "Remove one annoying thing": everyone picks a small friction point in the product or an internal process and fixes or prototypes a fix.
2. "Customer for a day": teams use the product as a new customer would and build improvements from what they find.
3. "Say it in one screen": teams pitch a new idea as a single mock-up plus a one-line value proposition.
4. "Make it work for everyone": accessibility and inclusion improvements, which suit designers, PMs and engineers alike.
5. "Kill a meeting": teams build something that replaces a recurring status update.

Option 1 usually gets the best turnout because the bar is low and the results are visible fast. Mixed teams of three or four, with at least one non-engineer each, will help keep it from becoming a coding contest.
love the kill a meeting one. how do we judge it

Keep it to three criteria: how many people the meeting involves, how believable the replacement is, and whether the team could actually use it next week. Give each a score out of five and let attendees vote in a quick round at the end, so it isn't left to a panel alone.
need ideas for finding out why users cancel after the first month. we've got survey data but it's thin

Thin survey data usually means people are skipping the questions or giving polite answers. Some ways to dig deeper:

- Short interviews with recent leavers. Even six to eight conversations can reveal patterns that a survey can't. Keep the tone curious, not defensive, and ask them to walk you through their first few weeks.
- Usage analysis. Compare what cancelled users did in their first seven days with what retained users did, and look for a key action that separates them.
- Cancellation flow questions. Replace a generic dropdown with two or three specific choices and one open text field.
- Support conversations. Tag the reasons that come up before cancellation.
- A check-in email at around day 20 asking, "What have you managed to do so far?" That tells you who is stuck before they leave.

I'd begin with the usage comparison and a handful of interviews, since together they tell you both what happened and why.
tagline for the app update. it's mostly about speed, loads twice as fast. needs to be short

Here are some options, from straightforward to more playful:

- Twice as fast. Zero extra effort.
- Blink and it's loaded.
- Faster by design.
- Less waiting. More doing.
- Quick off the mark.
- Same app. Double the speed.

I think "Less waiting. More doing." works best because it focuses on what the user gains rather than the technical improvement. If you want the number in there, "Same app. Double the speed." is accurate and punchy. Just make sure the "twice as fast" claim holds up across typical devices and connections, as people will notice if it doesn't.
Lucia wants to pilot some accessibility improvements. what small things could we start with that actually matter?

For a pilot it's best to choose changes that are small, visible and clearly useful. Some good starting points:

- Colour contrast: check that text and key buttons are easy to read against their backgrounds.
- Keyboard navigation: make sure someone can get through the main flow without a mouse, with a clear focus indicator.
- Screen reader labels: add meaningful labels to icons and buttons that currently have none.
- Error messages: say what went wrong and how to fix it, in text and not only through colour.
- Text resizing: confirm the layout still works when people increase their font size.
- Captions or transcripts for any video content.

I'd suggest picking keyboard navigation and labels for the main sign-up or purchase-free core flow first, since they tend to uncover the biggest blockers. Asking one or two people who use assistive technology to try it would give you far better insight than an internal checklist alone.
Arjun suggested a bug bash before the release. what makes those actually work? last one was chaos

Bug bashes tend to turn chaotic when nobody knows what to test and every report looks different. A few things help:

1. Give it a fixed time, ideally 60 to 90 minutes, with a clear start and finish.
2. Split people into small groups, each with a focus area such as sign-up, search or settings, so they aren't all clicking the same button.
3. Use one simple report template: what you did, what you expected, what happened, and a screenshot.
4. Have one person triage as reports arrive, merging duplicates and marking severity.
5. Add a bit of friendliness with a small prize for the most interesting find.

Also, ask the group to try unusual things, like a slow connection, a very long name or a different browser. Those tend to find the problems that the regular team misses. Finish by sharing the top five findings straight away so people see the value of taking part.

intro for the data analyst job post: "We're a fast-paced, dynamic startup looking for a rockstar analyst to join our family. You'll wear many hats and thrive in ambiguity. Must be a self-starter with a passion for data."

This is made almost entirely of phrases that candidates have learned to distrust. "Fast-paced," "rockstar," "family," "many hats" and "thrive in ambiguity" can suggest overwork and unclear roles, and they say nothing about the job. A good intro tells the candidate what they'll work on, who with and why it matters. Try: "We're looking for a data analyst to join our product team in London. You'll work directly with product managers and engineers to work out why people use, or stop using, our app, and your analysis will shape what we build next quarter. You'll have real ownership of our experimentation work, with support from a team that's still defining how it does analytics." That's honest about the ambiguity without making it sound like a selling point. It also filters for people who like the actual work rather than the buzzwords.

need to tell Felix Wong the API work is slipping. is this ok? "Hi Felix, so sorry to bother you, I know how busy you are and I really hate to do this, but I wanted to flag that there have been some challenges and the API work might possibly be delayed a little. Let me know your thoughts whenever."

The tone is kind, but the message buries what Felix needs, which is how late, why, and what you need from him. "Might possibly be delayed a little" will probably make him ask follow-up questions, and "whenever" gives him no sense of urgency. Put the news first, then the reason, then a specific ask. Draft: "Hi Felix, the API work will land about a week later than planned, so the new date is [date]. The cause is [reason, e.g. the auth changes needing a second round of testing]. Could we talk for 15 minutes on [day] about whether anything downstream needs to move? I'd rather sort it out now than have it surprise anyone later." One apology is enough, and in this version it's implied by the directness. Delivering bad news clearly is usually the more respectful thing to do.

vision para for the team doc, thoughts? "Our vision is to leverage cutting-edge AI to unlock synergies across the customer journey and deliver best-in-class, end-to-end experiences that empower users to achieve their goals."

Right now this could describe almost any software company, which is the main issue. "Leverage," "unlock synergies," "best-in-class," "end-to-end" and "empower" are filler, and nothing in the sentence would help your team decide what not to build. A strong vision statement is specific enough that someone could disagree with it. Start from who it's for and what changes for them. For example: "Anyone running a small business in the UK should be able to understand their finances in five minutes a week, without needing an accountant." Then add one sentence on how you'll get there, such as automating the boring parts first. If "AI" matters to the approach, name the job it does, like sorting receipts, rather than putting it in as a buzzword.
LinkedIn rec for Kwame Mensah, feels flat: "Kwame is a great person to work with. He is very hardworking and always delivers. I would recommend him to anyone."

It's kind, but a recommendation only helps him if it sounds like it came from someone who watched him work. "Great to work with," "hardworking" and "always delivers" could be about anyone. The fix is one concrete story plus the quality it shows. Think of a moment when Kwame did something others wouldn't have, such as untangling a messy handover, staying calm when a launch wobbled or explaining something technical clearly to non-engineers. Then write: "When [situation], Kwame [what he did], which meant [result]. He's the person I'd want on the team when things get complicated." Finish with who would benefit most from working with him, such as a team that needs someone steady in a scramble. Even three sentences with a real example will be much stronger than a generic paragraph.

slack announcement about the team change: "After careful consideration and in line with our evolving priorities, we are pleased to share that the onboarding squad will be undergoing a realignment, with certain responsibilities transitioning to new owners."

This sounds like a corporate memo, and people will mostly ask "so what does this mean for me?" The words "realignment," "transitioning" and "new owners" hide the actual news. In Slack, plain wording works better, and the first line should say what's changing and who is affected. Try: "Quick update on the onboarding squad: Lucia Romano is taking over as lead from Monday, and Nina Kowalski is moving to the payments-free growth work, so questions about onboarding experiments should go to Lucia. Nothing changes for the roadmap this quarter. If you're unsure who to ask about something, put it in this thread and we'll sort it out." Keep it short, name the people and say what stays the same. That tends to cut down on the side conversations that follow vague announcements.
payments-free growth?? that's weird

Yes, that phrase was my mistake and it doesn't belong there. Just say "the growth work" or whatever the team is actually called, so: "Nina Kowalski is moving to the growth team." Use the real name your colleagues already use so nobody has to guess.

opening of a blog post on prioritising: "Prioritisation is one of the most important and also one of the most difficult parts of product management, and there are many different frameworks and approaches that people use, each with their own advantages and disadvantages, so in this post I'm going to talk about some of them and what I think."

It's grammatical, but it's one very long sentence that announces the topic rather than making anyone want to read on. Phrases like "one of the most important" and "many different approaches" are things every reader already assumes. Start with something that's yours: a specific moment, a surprising opinion or a problem you faced. For example: "Last March I had 43 ideas, one team and room for about five. Every framework I tried gave me a different top five." Then promise what the post will do: "Here's what I learned about which frameworks help and which just make a decision look scientific." That gives the reader a story and a reason to continue in two short sentences.
ok but is 43 ideas too dramatic

Not if it's true, because a real number is more convincing than a round one. If the actual figure was 30 or 50, use that. If you're not sure, "nearly forty" is a fair way to say it. Just avoid exaggerating for effect, since readers can tell.
explain opportunity solution trees in plain english pls

It's a visual way to keep discovery work tied to a goal, from Teresa Torres's continuous discovery approach. At the top is one desired outcome, such as "increase the share of new users who set up a team in week one." Beneath it are opportunities, which are customer needs, pain points or desires you've heard in research, such as "I can't tell who has access." Under each opportunity you list several possible solutions, and under each solution the small experiments or assumption tests you could run. The point is to stop jumping from a problem to the first solution. It also makes you compare opportunities against one another and consider more than one idea for each. When someone proposes a pet feature, you can ask which opportunity it serves and which outcome that supports. Keep the tree to one outcome at a time, and update it after every round of interviews.
normally office mon wed, home tue thu fri. but its meant to hit 30 this week, esp weds and thurs. what would you do

Decide by what each day needs, not just by habit. Wednesday has the hiring panel, so if it works better in person, keep it as your office day, but plan to arrive early or late to dodge the hottest, most crowded Tube. If the panel can happen on video, working from home that day would save your energy for Thursday. Thursday is launch day, so being somewhere cool and calm with a good connection matters more than being in the building. Home is probably the better bet unless the team is gathering in person. Whichever you choose, carry water, wear something light, and avoid scheduling anything demanding for the late afternoon, when heat tends to hit hardest.
